PHSCS 587

Short-channel effects and DIBL

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows why a shorter channel allows source and drain fields to reach the gate-controlled interior

A long channel has an interior region controlled mainly by the gate. As channel length shrinks, source and drain boundary conditions influence more of that region. The potential is then inherently two-dimensional.

Each equipotential contour joins positions with the same electrostatic potential at one chosen operating bias. Closely spaced contours indicate a stronger local field, directed perpendicular to the contours toward lower potential. Changing drain bias produces a new contour map; comparing those maps reveals how the drain reshapes the source injection barrier.

Threshold rolloff describes a decrease in extracted threshold as channel length decreases at specified biases. Drain-induced barrier lowering, DIBL, describes the drain-bias-dependent lowering of the source injection barrier at fixed channel length. The two effects share electrostatic origins but are measured by different changes.

A common positive DIBL metric is −ΔVth/ΔVDS, stated with the threshold extraction method. Short-channel degradation can also worsen subthreshold swing. A simple barrier sketch alone does not predict a quantitative threshold or current.

Example

If an extracted threshold falls from 0.42 V to 0.38 V while drain voltage rises from 0.1 V to 0.9 V, the illustrative DIBL is 0.040/0.8 = 0.050 V/V, or 50 mV/V.

  • PHSCS 587 reading: 6.1–6.1.2.2, short-channel effect
  • PHSCS 587, 6.1–6.1.2.2 recording 2: equipotential maps, field directions and drain-induced barrier lowering.

Practice

1. How would you design two measurements to distinguish threshold rolloff from DIBL?

Choose which variable to hold fixed in each comparison.

For rolloff, compare devices of different channel length using the same drain bias and threshold definition. For DIBL, vary drain bias on the same device and use the same extraction method.
